title: Piecewise-linear approximations of multidimensional functions
contribution: Explicit MILP formulations (box SOS1 + simplex selection by plane binaries or by an SOS2 diagonal index) for piecewise-linear interpolation of lookup-table functions in 2 and 3 dimensions, with an empirical approximation-error study on camelback, a multilinear function and the EPA Complex Emissions Model.
problem_entry: Application-driven: gas-lift models use hydraulic lookup tables (non-analytic, piecewise-affine); her 1-D comparison recommended Keha et al., so extend explicit PWL formulations to n <= 3 and also use them to approximate generic NLPs by MILP (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Confine each point to one grid box (SOS1 per coordinate), then to one simplex (type-B triangulation with equal-volume simplices; plane binaries O(N^2), or SOS2 diagonal index O(N) in 2-D that allows irregular grids), and interpolate on the n+1 active vertices (pp. 6-22).
assumptions: Dimension <= 3 per lookup table (justified by cube-triangulation counts 1,2,5 vs 16,67,308,1493, p. 4); higher dimensions only via separable sums or bilinear/trilinear products of tables (pp. 4-5); equal spacing for the binary-plane method (p. 15); approximation only, no error bound.
proof_devices: Caratheodory-based uniqueness: n+2 equations in n+2 unknowns once n+1 vertices are active (pp. 5-6)
Table of vertices deactivated per plane binary; each pair lies on one edge, enabling edge-wise aggregated constraints (Table 1 p. 15; Eqs. 42-47 pp. 18-19)
Constraint/variable counting O(N^2) vs O(N) and 3 binaries vs 2(N1+N2+N3)+3 continuous (pp. 15-16, 21)
experiments: CPLEX 9.0.2/GAMS, Pentium 4; camelback (5 grids), 4-D multilinear (3 grids), 11-input EPA model (5 grids); error from 1e7 random samples (max/avg/std); optimisation results for the first two only; camelback lands in a non-global local minimum; no competitor formulation or solver (pp. 24-28).
positioning: Generalises the 1-D Floudas / Nemhauser-Wolsey construction (p. 6), borrows box-then-simplex from Zhang-Wang and the 2-D diagonal from Kosmidis et al. (pp. 6, 16); additive, non-critical; no Vielma-Ahmed-Nemhauser work in the reference list (pp. 28-31).
writing: Same contribution sentence in abstract and p. 2; constructive exposition with 10 figures and an implementer's equation summary (§5, pp. 22-24); two-sentence conclusion claiming good approximations for industrial models (p. 28).
limits_future: Stated: n <= 3 (p. 4) and equal spacing for method (a) (p. 15); unstated: no error bound, approximation local minima (p. 25), untested choice rule between the two simplex methods (p. 21); no future work (p. 28).

method_links.note: 2010 precursor: a data-defined (lookup-table) function is written as MILP constraints exploiting its piecewise-linear structure; no partner model or toolkit interface.
Grid level is a swept knob with errors reported per level, but there are no two textbook extremes and the trade-off between the two simplex-selection formulations is asserted, not measured.
Pre-2012 practice: three examples, no competitor, no verification; consistent with the SKILL dating Method 5 from 2012.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Dimension cap justified by a combinatorial count
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Lookup tables restricted to n <= 3 because cube triangulations need 16, 67, 308, 1493 simplices for n = 4-7.
1e7 random domain points per grid level; absolute/relative max, average, std reported next to optimisation results.
EPA-3 refines ETB/ETH only, because their acetaldehyde coefficients are about ten times larger; toxics error drops.

transferable: Use equal-volume (type B) triangulations so interpolation error is uniform; choose the orientation per function (pp. 10-12).
Tabulate which vertices each selection binary deactivates; if they share an edge, switch off whole edges with one aggregated constraint (pp. 15, 18-19).
SOS2 index over grid diagonals: O(N) constraints in 2-D and irregular grids finer where curvature is high (pp. 16, 19-21).
Estimate approximation quality with 1e7 random samples per grid level and refine only high-impact variables (pp. 25-28).

quotes.text: Noting the large number of simplices needed to partition hypercubes of dimension greater than three, this study restricts lookup tables to no more than three dimensions.
Note that, in this case, the approximation algorithm finds one of the non-global local minima, which is generated quickly.

title: Mathematical modeling and global optimization of large-scale extended pooling problems with the (EPA) complex emissions constraints
contribution: A leaner, law-faithful MINLP of pooling with the EPA Complex Emissions Model appended, a term-by-term MILP relaxation (piecewise bilinear, McCormick, range-uniform outer approximation, shifted edge-concave envelope, recursive arithmetic) and a C++ branch-and-bound that solves small to large (1104 continuous, 150 binary, 640 nonlinear terms) cases to <= 0.5% gap.
problem_entry: Regulation-driven: 40 CFR 80.45 fixes emissions formulas for reformulated gasoline; maximise blending profit on a pooling network under those limits; prior MINLP (Furman-Androulakis) single-fuel, redundant and partly unfaithful to the law (pp. 1-4).
key_idea: First read the legal model for structure (bilinear-looking extensions are exactly piecewise linear, Taylor extensions, redundant TAME and segment binaries), then relax each term class with the tightest cheap device and embed in B&B with OBBT on a coarse relaxation and node solves on a fine one (pp. 2-3, 9-25).
assumptions: Perfect mixing, linear blending except RVP (pp. 7-8); exact fuel qualities, uncertainty deferred (p. 8); summer case, additives blended at refinery, identical limits per product (pp. 25-26); law over spreadsheet (p. 3); N and N_OA fixed from experience on small/mid cases (p. 24).
proof_devices: Component-wise concavity test via second partials to decide edge-concavity (Eqs. 156-158, p. 23)

Shift alpha'4 = alpha4 + 3 alpha6 RVP^L + alpha7 MTB^L making the remainder edge-concave; remainder relaxed by vertex-polyhedral facets, correction by recursive arithmetic; 22% tighter (-10.61 vs -13.56) (pp. 23-24)
Range-uniform tangent points for monotone convex exponentials t(n) = ln(e^tL + n/N (e^tU - e^tL)) (Eqs. 153-155, pp. 22-23)
Recognition that apparently bilinear legal extensions are exactly piecewise linear and that NOX extensions are first-order Taylor expansions at breakpoints (pp. 3, 13, 17-18)
experiments: Three cases (Table 3, p. 25) in EPA Regions 1 and 2; Core 2 Quad 2.83 GHz serial, CPLEX 11.0 + MINOS 5.51; 1-11 nodes, 0.2-0.5% gaps, 4.5 s to 5274 s (Table 5, p. 27); Fig. 6 caption (487 s) disagrees with Table 5 (292/263 s); no competitor solver, no ablation beyond the 22% edge-concave figure; all instance data in Appendices B-D.
positioning: Generous pooling history (pp. 3-4); precise, example-backed criticism of Furman-Androulakis for disjunctions found in neither the law nor the spreadsheet (pp. 2-3); relaxation choice backed by the group's own comparative study (p. 21).
writing: Numbered four-point justification of the new formulation in the introduction (pp. 2-3); size headline repeated in abstract, introduction and conclusion (pp. 1, 2, 29); equation-heavy (161 equations); no limits paragraph (p. 29).
limits_future: Passing limits: no uncertainty (p. 8), simplified additive logistics (p. 25), parameters from small cases (p. 24); unstated: 0.5% tolerance, no competitors, Region 1 large case 13x slower than Region 2 unexplained (Table 5, p. 27); no future work.

method_links.note: Reads the law's formulas for structure missed by the earlier model: exact piecewise-linear extensions, Taylor-expansion extensions, redundant TAME tracking and segment binaries, an edge-concave remainder; each structure is exploited in the relaxation.
Piecewise relaxation of u*of terms dropped because it raised whole-solve time without changing the objective.
Partition levels N and N_OA are levers but fixed from experience on small/mid cases with no sweep; robustness only asserted for the large case.
Pre-2012 evaluation: no competitors, 0.5% tolerance, inconsistent CPU time between Fig. 6 and Table 5; public instance parameters are the one auditor-like element.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Primary-source fidelity audit of a predecessor model
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Diffs Furman-Androulakis against 40CFR80.45 and the EPA spreadsheet, lists invented disjunctions (Delta E200 at 65.52 vol%), follows the law where sources disagree.
Subtract a bound-calibrated cubic term so the remainder is component-wise concave; 22% tighter lower bound than recursive arithmetic.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Coarse relaxation for bound tightening, fine relaxation for node bounds
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: OBBT with N = 1 (McCormick) and N_OA = 8; node solved with N = 16.

transferable: Diff a predecessor's model of a standard against the primary legal text; follow the primary source where they disagree (p. 3).
Model k breakpoints with k disjunction binaries rather than k+1 segment binaries (pp. 2-3).
Place outer-approximation tangent points evenly over the function's range for steep exponentials (pp. 22-23).
Shift a non-edge-concave polynomial by a bound-calibrated term to obtain an edge-concave remainder with a vertex-polyhedral envelope (p. 23).
Run OBBT on a coarse relaxation and solve nodes on a fine one (p. 24).
Publish all instance parameters in appendices so the application instance becomes a benchmark (pp. 35-38).
coauthors: Chrysanthos E. Gounaris, Christodoulos A. Floudas

title: APOGEE: Global optimization of standard, generalized, and extended pooling problems via linear and logarithmic partitioning schemes
contribution: A logarithmic (base-2) MILP encoding of the piecewise McCormick relaxation of bilinear terms, compared with the linear nf4r scheme inside a full branch-and-bound on 25 pooling problems at 7 partition levels, plus the free APOGEE tool for standard, generalized and extended pooling; the linear scheme stays the default.
problem_entry: Two prior large-scale pooling studies used piecewise relaxations with linearly many binaries; Vielma-Nemhauser's logarithmic PWL models suggested a port to relaxations; also unify three pooling classes in one tool (pp. 1-3).
key_idea: Encode the active segment of disjunctive program (6) by ceil(log2 N_P) binaries with paired continuous copies and slacks so continuous variables also scale logarithmically, add a sharpening cut when N_P is not a power of two, and judge it inside the whole algorithm rather than at the root (pp. 14-23).
assumptions: Uniform partitioning of one variable per bilinear term (p. 13); no specialised branching for the log encoding (p. 23); pool-pool cycles excluded in the generalized class (p. 4); minimum-flow semicontinuity (p. 13).
proof_devices: Worked activation examples (N_P = 4, x = xL + 2.6a; N_P = 5, x = xL + 3.6a) in place of an equivalence proof (Figs. 6-9, pp. 17-20)
Redundancy by pairwise subtraction: segment constraint (8) implied by (10a)-(10d), and (11) by (14) (pp. 18, 21)
Closed-form size accounting per scheme (Tables 4-5, pp. 16, 23) explaining why N_P = 5 costs as much as N_P = 8 plus a cut (p. 29)
experiments: 25 literature pooling problems with known optima (Table 3, p. 9) x N_P in {3,4,5,6,8,12,16} x {linear, log} inside Algorithm 1; Xeon E5520, CPLEX 12.1, SNOPT 5.3, 7200 s; tolerances 1e-6/1e-3/1e-2 (stated why); wins counted with a 10% tie rule; log wins for N_P >= 8, linear for small N_P, N_P = 4 best on 20/25; three non-converged runs listed; numerical difficulty on three large instances; no competitor solvers; Table 6 log rows for EPA Small/Med inconsistent (pp. 22-30).
positioning: Broad generous survey (pp. 3-7); explicit consistent-vs-different statement against Vielma-Nemhauser (p. 19); Li et al. criticised as not sharp via Vielma et al. 2010b (pp. 6-7); frames results as robustness evidence for Vielma's claims beyond isolated MILPs (p. 29).
writing: Judging principle stated before results (p. 23); balanced reading of Table 8 ending in a decision against her own novelty (pp. 29-30); hedged conjecture for other classes (p. 31); user-facing tool section (pp. 30-31); abstract slip on what the binaries scale with (p. 1).
limits_future: Specific: novelty loses at the partition levels that work best for pooling; numerical difficulty on Meyer 10/15 and EPA Large R1; two EPA problems not solved to 1e-3 (pp. 29-30); future: classes needing finer partitions (p. 31).

method_links.note: Relaxations judged inside the APOGEE algorithm rather than at the root; verdict split by partition regime; stability makes the linear scheme the default against her own logarithmic novelty.
Partition-level family swept over 7 levels on 25 problems with both encodings; robustness claim that guessing the partition is not crucial; no selection rule beyond using N_P = 4.
Weak: Algorithm 2 turns structural counts (bilinear terms of p vs q, variable-set sizes) into an automatic formulation and partition choice.
Large documented test set with known optima, exact hardware/versions, tie rule and listed failures, but no competitor solvers or independent verification; Table 6 anomaly unexplained.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Port a neighbouring community's formulation trick into relaxations and test its claim inside a full solver
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Vielma-Nemhauser logarithmic PWL models carried to piecewise McCormick relaxations; result presented as robustness evidence for their claim beyond isolated MILPs.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: 10%-tie win counting over a problems x parameter x formulation grid
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Table 8 counts wins per formulation and per partition level, treating times within 10% of the best as ties.
ceil(log2 5) = ceil(log2 8), so N_P = 5 carries N_P = 8's size plus a cut, explaining why log does better at powers of two.

transferable: Base-2 encoding of the active partition in a piecewise McCormick relaxation, with logarithmically many continuous copies and slacks (pp. 18-22).
Prove a selection constraint redundant by pairwise subtraction of envelope inequalities and drop it (p. 18).
Evaluate a relaxation by swapping only that component inside the full B&B over a parameter grid; count wins with a 10% tie rule; list every non-converged run (pp. 22-30).
Choose formulation and partitioned variable set automatically from term counts (p. 25).
Release the solver with the test suite preloaded in a GUI and warn users about instance size and timing variability (pp. 23, 30-31).
coauthors: Jeffrey P. Thompson, Christodoulos A. Floudas
